title: AlphaGo's Move 37
hook: The Go move that experts called a mistake, until it won the game.
peek: In 2016, in the second game of its match against Lee Sedol, the program AlphaGo played a move that human experts would almost never consider. Commentators were baffled. It turned out to be the key to the game.
lede: In March 2016 DeepMind's AlphaGo played Lee Sedol, one of the strongest Go players in the world, in a five-game match in Seoul. On the 37th move of the second game, it placed a stone in a spot that convention treats as too loose. Commentators assumed it was an error. By the end of the game, it looked like insight.

bullets.text: The stone pressed diagonally against one of Lee's stones from the fifth line. Tradition favours the third and fourth lines for such moves, since a higher one seems to hand the opponent safe ground along the edge.
AlphaGo's own estimate was that a human player would choose that move about one time in ten thousand. It played it anyway, because its search rated the move's long-term value highly.
Lee took around a quarter of an hour to reply. He went on to lose the game, and AlphaGo won the match four games to one.
Fan Hui, the European champion whom AlphaGo had beaten months earlier, was watching in Seoul. He said it was not a human move, and called it beautiful.
